name: competing-consumers
intent: Let a pool of identical consumers share one point-to-point channel so processing throughput scales with the number of consumers, bursts are absorbed by the queue, and a failed consumer loses its unacknowledged work to the surviving pool.
problem: A single consumer on a queue cannot keep up with the arrival rate, and it is a single point of failure as well: messages pile up, latency grows, and a crash stalls the stream. Senders must not know how many consumers exist, and consumers must not have to coordinate with one another.
context: Asynchronous messaging where each message is an independent unit of work and the channel is a point-to-point queue - an in-process queue or a brokered queue (JMS/AMQP queue, Amazon SQS, a Kafka partition or consumer group). The channel, not the sender and not an application dispatcher, owns the decision which consumer receives each message; the pattern presumes messages may be processed out of order and more than once.
benefits: Throughput scales with the pool: attaching more consumers to the same queue raises concurrent processing without changing producers or the message contract.
Availability by replication: the unacknowledged messages of a crashed consumer are redelivered to its peers, so one failure does not stall the stream.
Load levelling: the queue absorbs bursts and each consumer pulls at its own pace, so one slow message cannot block the other consumers the way it would block a single reader.
No coordination code: the channel's atomic hand-off replaces dispatchers, leader election and sharded assignment, and every consumer stays identical and stateless.
Elastic operations: consumers start, stop or autoscale on queue depth and consumer lag without any producer-side knowledge, which is how cloud queues and Kafka consumer groups are operated.
tradeoffs: Message ordering is destroyed: once several consumers run, processing order no longer matches enqueue order, and FIFO guarantees hold only per partition (Kafka) or per message group (sessions).

At-least-once delivery becomes visible: a consumer that dies after doing part of its work receives the message again, so handlers must be idempotent or the duplicate neutralised with dedupe keys or transactions.

Poison messages multiply their damage: a message that kills its consumer is redelivered to the next one, so delivery caps, dead-lettering and alerting are part of the pattern rather than optional extras.

The shared channel becomes the bottleneck and single point of failure: if the broker cannot sustain the aggregate rate, extra consumers buy nothing, and an unavailable queue stops the whole pool at once.

Observability and fairness need deliberate work: which consumer handled a given message is unknown a priori (correlation identifiers and tracing are mandatory), and unbounded prefetch lets one greedy consumer hoard messages and starve its peers.

participants.responsibility: Creates messages and writes them to the queue; knows the channel identity only, never how many consumers exist or which one will handle a given message.
Buffers messages, hands each one to exactly one of the competing consumers, and tracks acknowledgement and redelivery so no two consumers process the same message at the same time.
One of N identical instances that takes the next available message, processes it independently, and acknowledges or rejects it; holds no state another consumer would need.
Persists the queue, enforces atomic delivery, redelivery, delivery caps and dead-lettering, and manages consumer-group membership across processes and hosts.
The payload in transit, carrying identity and metadata - idempotency key, correlation identifier, attempt count - that make redelivery, duplicate detection and tracing survivable.

use_cases: Job queues behind a web tier: HTTP requests enqueue email, report or image work and a pool of worker processes drains the queue.
Cloud autoscaling consumers: Azure Functions with Service Bus queue triggers, SQS plus Lambda, or Kubernetes workers scaled on queue depth - a burst of messages starts more consumers.
Kafka consumer groups: the members of one group compete for partition-level point-to-point channels, one consumer per partition at most.
Long-running integrations that must survive restarts: messages unacknowledged at the moment of a crash are redelivered to the surviving consumers instead of dying with the process.
Legacy batch processing where N identical daemons pull from one durable queue and throughput is raised simply by starting more daemons.
Event-driven microservices with independent command handling: each microservice instance competes to process commands from a shared queue without requiring service-discovery or load balancers.
Image/video processing pipelines: heavy media transcoding tasks are distributed across a worker pool, with failures triggering automatic redistribution to available workers.
Payment and order processing: charge authorization requests are distributed to multiple processors for horizontal scaling, with idempotency keys preventing duplicate transactions.

Celery worker fleets: several worker processes (each with --concurrency slots) consume one broker queue; worker_prefetch_multiplier caps how many tasks each worker reserves so slow tasks cannot hoard the queue.

RabbitMQ consumer pools: multiple consumers on one classic queue with per-consumer prefetch (basic.qos) bound each worker's unacknowledged batch, and the consumer capacity metric tells operators when adding consumers will actually raise throughput.

AWS SQS worker fleets: each worker's ReceiveMessage hides the message from peers for the visibility timeout; if the worker dies or overruns the timeout the message reappears for another consumer, so handlers dedupe on a business key.
avoid_when: Every interested consumer must see the message: use a publish-subscribe channel or an event topic - extra subscribers on a queue silently steal messages instead of receiving copies.
Strict ordering across messages is required: keep a single consumer, or partition (Kafka) or session (Service Bus) by key and accept ordering only within a key.
Work items depend on each other or must be aggregated: split explicitly and combine with correlation, aggregator and resequencer patterns instead of hoping the pool preserves order.
A single in-process worker on a plain task queue is enough: no broker, no pool and no delivery semantics to design.
anti_patterns: Attaching a second logical consumer (audit listener, cache invalidator) to the same queue and expecting publish-subscribe semantics - messages are stolen, not copied.
Scaling consumers without idempotency: a crash mid-handler causes redelivery and double side effects such as charging a card twice.
Poison-message loops: an always-failing message redelivered forever because no delivery cap or dead-letter channel exists.
More Kafka consumers than partitions, or a bigger pool in front of an already saturated broker: idle consumers presented as scalability.
Acknowledging before the work completes (auto-ack, unbounded prefetch) so a crash loses acknowledged work while one consumer hoards messages and starves the rest of the pool.
Ignoring correlation identifiers: without tracing metadata, it is impossible to determine which consumer processed a given message or diagnose processing chains.
Hot-partition bottleneck: using a naive partition key causes one partition to receive disproportionate traffic, nullifying the benefit of parallel consumers.
design_principles: Single responsibility: consumers process, the channel decides delivery; the routing policy lives in one place instead of in every sender.
Late binding and dependency inversion: producers depend on the queue abstraction, never on consumer identities, locations or count.
Replica homogeneity: competing consumers must be interchangeable; heterogeneous work needs routing, not competition.
Idempotency and statelessness: any message may arrive twice or out of order, so handlers must be safe to repeat and must not depend on other messages.
Explicit flow control: bound the queue and each consumer's unacknowledged budget (prefetch) rather than letting overload become memory or backlog growth.
Observable by design: include correlation IDs and trace context in every message so processing paths can be reconstructed.
best_practices: Make handlers idempotent (dedupe on message id or an idempotency key) and state the delivery guarantee before adding the second consumer.
Cap delivery attempts and route poison messages to a dead-letter channel with alerting and a replay path.
Size the pool to the real bottleneck - broker throughput, partition count, downstream rate limits - and autoscale on queue depth or consumer lag.
Acknowledge after processing, bound prefetch or unacknowledged messages per consumer, and set visibility timeouts above the p99 handler latency.
Design for out-of-order processing, or partition by entity key when per-entity order is mandatory.
Drain gracefully: stop pulling, finish in-flight messages, then exit, so redelivery stays the exception rather than the shutdown path.
Use composite deduplication keys (consumer identity + message identity) when multiple independent consumers share the channel, not message identity alone.
Set queue capacity and backpressure signals so producers slow down before the broker is overwhelmed.
Choose partition keys carefully to avoid hot partitions; prefer high-cardinality keys that distribute load evenly.
Implement structured logging with correlation IDs on every message to trace processing across consumer instances.
Monitor consumer lag, queue depth, and redelivery rates as primary operational signals.
Use PeekLock or equivalent receive semantics in brokered deployments: the message is locked during processing and released only on explicit ack or abandon.
Design for at-least-once delivery; treat exactly-once as a downstream concern handled by idempotency.
Test poison-message handling by injecting deliberately malformed messages and verifying dead-letter routing.
Consider transactional outbox when messages must be published atomically with database changes.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Competing Consumers (Messaging Endpoints chapter).
